artboards.title: B · The Deck (grid of live cards)
A · Agent mode in the rail

annotations.text:
Overall look — every value lifted from src/style.css, so this is the app as it is, plus one new thing: a 38px header bar.

Today every menu hangs off a right-click or a status chip. The header gives Shell / Panes / Project / View a fixed home, puts ⌘K search in reach, and gives Settings a permanent gear.

One popup shape for all of them: 14px radius, pill rows, shortcut right-aligned in mono, destructive row last and red.

Rule: a row is a verb, a shortcut or a colour. Anything needing a form ends in “…” and opens Settings on that section.

The separated settings window you asked for: its own window, sidebar of sections, no more one-wide-row-per-field.

Every field config.json holds today is here — font, size, scrollback, default folder and profile, accent and the full 16-colour palette, rail width and collapse, reopen-tabs, update source and token, quota budgets, plus Profiles / Accounts / Hosts / Projects as list editors.

Rows marked NEW SETTING are ones the app does not store yet (cursor style, right-click, transparency, dim panes, check-on-launch) — they are the proposal, not a description.

Changes write straight to config.json; no Apply button, and the file stays hand-editable.

The pattern for everything you can create: list on the left, one form on the right, Duplicate and Delete on every row, deletes undoable.

Profiles, Accounts, SSH hosts and Projects all use this same screen — Accounts is shown because it has the most in it.
Kept as a sketch, not built out: settings living in the rail as a pinned row instead of a separate window. Say if you would rather have this and I will take it to the same fidelity.

Tier 1 from the audit: the rail lists names, it should list states.

With a dozen Claude Code sessions the binding question every half minute is "which one is waiting for me?" — and the only way to answer it today is to visit each tab. A collapsed project can hide a session that has been waiting for ten minutes.

All the plumbing exists: every byte already passes through one callback in pane.ts, and paint() already repaints the rail. What this needs is a 14px slot, four glyphs, and a rail that patches rows instead of rebuilding them.

The placement decision, with the two rejected options kept so the reasoning survives.

A wins because the left edge of a rail row already carries two other meanings (the project rule, the focus bar) and the row background already carries two more (active, project colour). The right end is the only unclaimed real estate, and it is where the pane badge and capture dot already sit.

Should OBPTerm have an agent pane like NodeTerm?

My honest read: NodeTerm's canvas exists to make many agents visible at once — that is the part worth taking. The canvas itself (draggable nodes, ropes) would fight the rail and turn the terminal into an orchestrator, which the audit fenced off.

Three directions, different in kind, all fed by the hook data v0.9.0 already collects (state, activity line, last message, pending permission, context %, session id):

B — THE DECK (left, my pick): a special tab, Ctrl+G. A live card per Claude session: state, the tail of what it said, Allow/Deny and question options inline, context meter. Click = jump to the real tab. This is NodeTerm's overview without the canvas. Cost: M — the card tails come straight from the host's ring, no second terminal needed.

A — AGENT MODE IN THE RAIL: no new surface at all. One toggle widens the rail to ~336px and swaps tab rows for supervision cards; the pane area is untouched. Cheapest, always visible, but competes with the tab list and caps out around 8 agents.

C — TRIAGE FLOW: not a place, a motion. Ctrl+J walks everything that needs you, loudest first — full-width card, A/D/Enter/Space, then the next. Best keystrokes-per-decision of the three; useless for ambient awareness, so it pairs with A or B rather than replacing them.

They compose: B is the home, C is the motion (Ctrl+J works from anywhere), A is the glanceable summary that stays when the Deck tab is not open.

If you want one: build B, add C in the same release (it is the same data with a different frame), skip A.

The pick, honestly:
A is the safe premium floor. B is the one that makes 10-agent supervision FEEL better, not just look better. C photographs best but fights the flat Sentinel doctrine.

A + B compose: ship A's micro-motion as the base layer and B's event choreography on top. C's sheen could be borrowed as a one-off for tab activation only.

Each board has a Replay button — hover things too.

The decision page. Three rows, three options each — answer with one per row, e.g. "O2 / O2 / O3".

My recommendation: O2 / O2 / O3 — the tab language, sheen-on-focus, choreographed deck. One consistent vocabulary (the knock means the same thing in the rail and the deck), one-shot flourishes everywhere else, idle stays perfectly still.

Everything here keeps the current layout, projects, colors and the bottom bar untouched. All animations are transform/opacity — cheap at 10 live tabs.

(The earlier exploration pages for motion and agent views remain in the page menu for reference; the front-page directions were discarded as requested.)

Three surfaces for 'this is where my day runs', all one keypress from the terminal, none replacing it. All are built from data the host ALREADY has (hooks, transcripts, diffstats, quota) — no new collection.

D1 MISSION CONTROL (Ctrl+Home) — the day as a board: Needs you / Running / Done-today review queue, plus an hour-by-hour activity strip with quota projection. The morning and return-to-desk surface. (Steals: Warp's triage columns, Superset's review queue.)

D2 THREADS (Ctrl+T) — sessions as conversations: Claude's answers as readable text, your reply box inline, Fork on every card. Work through words, not scrollback. (Steals: NodeTerm's branch-a-conversation + reply-without-attaching.)

D3 THE WIRE (Ctrl+E) — a chronological feed of everything the fleet did (asks, dones, errors, test passes, merges, quota notices) with inline actions and filters. The catch-up surface. (Steals: CI-feed ergonomics nobody has put in a terminal yet.)

My take: D1 and D3 answer different moments (start of a block vs return from away) — D2 is the boldest reframe and the closest to how you actually work. If forced to one: THREADS, with the Wire's feed as its left rail later.

The two views, final naming:

LIST VIEW — the better-visualized evolution of today's rail: filter + count, square dots, ctx% pill per row, state in words, and the ×N chip unfolding each session's agents inline with their live tool feeds. The daily driver.

NODE VIEW — the other level: sessions as state-tinted nodes (RUNNING / NEEDS YOU / DONE), the permission prompt answerable ON the node, AGENT cards with live tool feeds hanging off computed edges (bottom-center of parent to top-center of child — always attached, they follow the cards through layout and zoom), dashed ORIGIN node, minimap + zoom + quota chrome. Auto-layout, pan/zoom, no dragging.

Ctrl+M toggles. Same data feed, same answer keys. Build order: List View first (it upgrades the rail you use all day), Node View second on the same plumbing. Run Ledger discarded.

Answers settled 2026-08-26: nodes are LIVE (answer/reply/scroll on the node; click promotes to a real terminal in place); nodes are born from events with one-shot entrance motion (edge draws itself, node scales in from the parent's anchor); node types v1 = SESSION / AGENT / SHELL / ORIGIN, later DIFF / NOTE / TRIGGER. Ctrl+G opens the surface (replacing the deck), Ctrl+M flips the view.

Replacing the Agents button with something that both OPENS and SWITCHES.

A · Segmented — words, no learning curve, the lit half tells you what Ctrl+G will open. Costs ~64px of row width, so the loudest-hold subtitle truncates sooner in the alert state.

B · Icon pair — narrowest (48px), subtitle keeps its width, but 'which glyph is which' takes one look to learn.

C · Two destinations — most discoverable and matches how projects already expand into rows; adds two rows of rail height permanently.

My pick: A. The row is a switcher only in appearance — the badge, subtitle and Ctrl+G behaviour are untouched, and words beat glyphs on a control you touch a few times a day. If the alert subtitle feels cramped in practice, B is the same design with the labels swapped for glyphs.
